module_title: Peasant and Tribal Uprisings - Key Movements, Acts, and Literature
introduction: At this level, we look at earlier uprisings like the Sanyasi rebellion, the shift towards legal resistance in the late 19th century (Pabna revolt), and the specific legislative acts the British were forced to pass to calm the uprisings.

core_concepts.title: Sanyasi Rebellion (1763-1800)
core_concepts.description: Occurred in Bengal after the devastating famine of 1770. Displaced peasants, demobilized soldiers, and religious monks (Sanyasis and Fakirs) joined hands to fight the British and Zamindars.

core_concepts.title: Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873-76)
core_concepts.description: Unlike earlier violent revolts, peasants in Pabna (Bengal) formed leagues to fight oppressive Zamindars through legal means and rent strikes. They declared they wanted to be 'the Queen's, and Queen's ryots only'.

core_concepts.title: Deccan Riots (1875)
core_concepts.description: Peasants in the Deccan region (Maharashtra) revolted against greedy Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders. They primarily targeted debt bonds and account books, destroying them to erase debt records.

core_concepts.title: Kol Mutiny (1831)
core_concepts.description: The Kols of Chhotanagpur rebelled against the transfer of their lands to outsider Sikh and Muslim farmers by the local Hindu, Muslim, and Sikh moneylenders.

important_entities.name: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
important_entities.significance: His famous novel 'Anandamath' (which contains the national song 'Vande Mataram') is based on the background of the Sanyasi Rebellion.

important_entities.name: Buddho Bhagat
important_entities.significance: Led the widespread armed uprising of the Kol tribes before being killed in battle by the British.

important_entities.name: Majnum Shah and Bhavani Pathak
important_entities.significance: Key figures who organized the displaced populations in Bengal to conduct guerrilla warfare against the East India Company.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Students often group Pabna with violent revolts. However, the Pabna movement was remarkably peaceful, focusing on legal battles and rent-strikes rather than armed conflict.
The Deccan Riots were not directed against the British directly, but rather against the indigenous moneylender class (Sahukars) who trapped farmers in debt.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Connects Sanyasi Rebellion with the book 'Anandamath' and Indigo Revolt with the play 'Neel Darpan'.

exam_strategy_tips: Match the Following questions frequently pair rebellions with their geographic locations (e.g., Kols -> Chhotanagpur, Pabna -> Bengal, Deccan Riots -> Maharashtra).
Remember that the Deccan Riots led to the passing of the 'Deccan Agriculturists Relief Act' of 1879.
